items.explanation: Constructive means criticism that builds toward improvement, which all three clauses require: it targets the plan not the person, it offers a better way, and it was acted on. Supportive and helpful are general goodwill without the critical element, and encouraging is about morale, not about the substance of the work.
items.question: Choose the word nearest in meaning to the word in the sentence. His criticism was ___: it attacked the plan, never the person who wrote it, it offered a better way to do the work, and the author adopted one of its suggestions.

items.explanation: Mitigated means made the damage less severe, which both clauses require: the flooding did not end, so the harm was reduced rather than removed, and the improvement lasted, so it is a lasting lessening of harm. Improved is vague and does not carry the lessening of harm. Relieved would mean removed the trouble, which is too strong since the flooding did not end, and aggravated is the opposite, meaning made worse.
items.question: Choose the word nearest in meaning to the word in the sentence. The new drainage did not end the flooding, but it ___ the damage in the old quarter enough for shops to reopen, and the improvement lasted through the next monsoon.

items.explanation: Reticent means unwilling to speak freely, saying little rather than volunteering more. Only the first sentence shows that: the witness answers in single words and says nothing beyond what he was asked. Describing the accident in detail to every reporter, volunteering a long account, and shouting a version across the room are all the opposite of reticence.
options: The reticent witness answered in single words and said nothing beyond what he was asked.
The reticent witness described the accident in detail to every reporter who asked.
The reticent witness volunteered a long account before anyone asked him.
The reticent witness shouted his version of events across the room.
items.question: Which sentence uses the word RETICENT correctly?

items.explanation: A double-edged sword is something that has both a good and a bad effect. Here the benefit is lower costs and the harm is the loss of error checks, and both come from the same change, the automation itself.
options: The automation is dangerous and should be avoided.
The automation is expensive and not worth buying.
The automation has both a benefit and a harm, and the two come from the same change.
The automation cuts costs in two departments at once.
items.question: The new automation cuts costs, but it removes the checks a junior used to catch errors, so the same change helps and harms at once. The manager says the automation is a double-edged sword. Which of the following best explains what the manager means?

items.explanation: Resolute means firm and purposeful, which all three clauses require: she holds her position through six rounds, yet she changes it where the figures prove her wrong, and she does so without threats. Stubborn, obstinate and intransigent all describe refusing to change, and the second clause rules them out: a stubborn negotiator would not change on the point where the figures were wrong. Only resolute carries firmness that still answers to evidence.
items.question: Choose the word that best fits the sentence. The negotiator was ___: she held her position through six rounds, she changed it on the one point where the other side showed her figures were wrong, and she did so without raising her voice or threatening to walk out.

items.explanation: 'Each' is singular, so it takes 'has submitted'. 'None' takes the singular 'has' here, since the sense is 'not one of them has been interviewed'. The panel's work began last week, a finished past event, so it needs the simple past 'began', and 'begun' would need an auxiliary such as 'has'. Only the first option satisfies all three rules.
items.question: Fill in the blanks: Each of the candidates ___ submitted a form, and none of them ___ been interviewed yet, although the panel ___ its work last week.

items.explanation: Forecast means a formal published prediction of a future quantity with a stated figure, which both clauses require: the prediction rests on survey data, and the fall is given as a single published figure, 8%. Projected describes extending a past trend line, which the stem rules out in so many words. Predicted is general and carries no published-figure sense, and anticipated states an expectation without a figure. The key is therefore forecast, and the added clause removes the old ambiguity with projected.
items.question: Fill in the blank: The report, based on the survey data, ___ that demand would fall if prices rose further, and it gave the fall as a single published figure, 8% for the next quarter, rather than extending the past trend line.

items.explanation: In 'one of the managers who were present', the relative pronoun 'who' refers to 'one', which is singular, so the verb must be 'was', not 'were', and part B is wrong. The same one-of rule is applied correctly at the end, where 'one of them later withdrew it' uses the singular form. The solver must apply the rule twice: it fails in B and holds at the end.
items.question: Find the part with an error: (A) One of the managers (B) who were present (C) raised (D) an objection, and one of them later withdrew it.

items.explanation: The first blank needs 'accept', meaning to come to terms with the loss. The second needs 'except', meaning apart from the fact that two smaller contracts were also ending. Using 'except' in the first blank would make no sense, and 'accept' in the second would claim the team agreed with the fact rather than setting it aside, so only the first option fits both.
items.question: Fill in the blanks: The team could not ___ the loss of its biggest contract without a plan, ___ for the fact that two smaller contracts were also ending.

items.explanation: P follows S1 because it starts the seasonal cycle in spring. Q follows P because the mustard honey comes from the mustard fields in P. T follows Q because the wax is left after the May harvest and must be sold before the hives move on in June, which R describes. R follows T because the return to the orchard happens in June, and S follows R because 'there' is the orchard in R. PQRST puts the wax sale after the hives have already moved on, and PRQTS puts the return before the harvest that precedes it.
items.question: S1: A beekeeper's year follows the flowering seasons. S6: By winter the hives are sealed and the beekeeper waits for spring. Arrange P, Q, R, S, T in proper order. P. In spring the hives are moved to the mustard fields. Q. The mustard honey is harvested in May. R. By June the hives return to the orchard. S. There they gather nectar until the monsoon. T. The wax left after the May harvest is sold before the hives move on in June.

items.explanation: The first differences are 6, 8, 10, 12, rising by 2 each time, so the next differences are 14 and 16. The next two terms are 43 + 14 = 57 and 57 + 16 = 73, and their sum is 57 + 73 = 130. 57 alone is only the first missing term, and stopping after one difference misses the second step entirely.
items.question: Find the next term in the series, and then the term after that: 7, 13, 21, 31, 43, ?, ?. What is the sum of the two missing terms?
items.topic: Analytical and Logical Reasoning - Number Series

items.explanation: Alternate terms form two series: 5, 9, 13 increase by 4, and 8, 11 increase by 3. The next term continues the second series: 11 + 3 = 14.
items.question: Find the next term in the series: 5, 8, 9, 11, 13, ?
items.topic: Analytical and Logical Reasoning - Number Series

items.explanation: The operations alternate: add 1, then multiply by 2, then add 1, then multiply by 2. So 5 + 1 = 6, 6 x 2 = 12, 12 + 1 = 13, 13 x 2 = 26, 26 + 1 = 27, 27 x 2 = 54, and the next operation is add 1, giving 55.
items.question: Find the next term in the series: 5, 6, 12, 13, 26, 27, 54, ?
items.topic: Analytical and Logical Reasoning - Number Series

items.explanation: The gaps increase by 1: the gaps are 3, 4, 5, 6, so the next gaps are 7 and 8. S plus 7 is Z, and Z plus 8 is H. Z is only the sixth term, so stopping after one step lands on it, and the other options are one letter either side of the seventh term.
items.question: Find the next letter in the series, and then the letter after that: A, D, H, M, S, ?, ?. What is the second of the two missing letters, the seventh term of the series?
items.topic: Analytical and Logical Reasoning - Letter Series

items.explanation: S moves 2 places to U, T moves 4 places to X, O moves 6 places to U, N moves 8 places to V and E moves 10 places to O, giving UXUVO. Reversing the whole word gives OVUXU.
items.question: In a code, letters are shifted forward by 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 places in order and the result is then reversed. How is STONE written in this code?
items.topic: Analytical and Logical Reasoning - Coding Decoding

items.explanation: The first letters descend by 2 (R, P, N, L, J), the digits rise by 1, and the third letter sits 3, 7, 11, 15, 19 places after the first letter, so the gap itself grows by 4. The missing term is therefore NO#3Y4~4. NO#3X4~4 and NO#3Z4~4 get the easy progressions right and guess the accelerating rule, and LO#3Y4~4 slips one step on the first letter. NO#3Y4~4 is not among the options, so the correct answer is 'None of these'.
items.question: Find the missing term in the sequence: RS#1U2~2, PQ#2W3~3, ______, LM#4[5~5, JK#5]6~6.
items.topic: Analytical and Logical Reasoning - Coding Decoding

items.explanation: S and U are both children of T, so they are siblings, and R, as S's wife, is U's sister-in-law. U is married to V and V is the mother of W, so W is U's child, and R, as the sibling-in-law of W's father, is W's aunt by marriage. 'Sister-in-law' describes R's relation to U, not to W, and 'daughter-in-law' would require R to be married to W, which she is not.
items.question: R is the wife of S. S is the son of T. T is the father of U. U is married to V, and V is the mother of W. How is R related to W?
items.topic: Analytical and Logical Reasoning - Blood Relations

items.explanation: G is D's daughter and D is B's son, so G is A's great-granddaughter. F is married to G, so F is A's great-grandson-in-law. 'Grandson-in-law' is one generation too close, and 'son-in-law' two generations too close.
items.question: A is the father of B. B has two sons, C and D. C is married to E. E's brother F is married to D's daughter G. How is F related to A?
items.topic: Analytical and Logical Reasoning - Blood Relations

items.explanation: 27, 36, 45 and 54 are all multiples of 9 with digit sum 9: 27, 36, 45 and 54 are 9 x 3, 9 x 4, 9 x 5 and 9 x 6. 57 is a multiple of 3 but not of 9, and its digit sum is 12, so it is the only one failing both conditions at once. Checking divisibility by 3 alone leaves 57 looking ordinary, which is why both conditions must be checked.
items.question: Find the odd one out: 27, 36, 45, 54, 57.
items.topic: Analytical and Logical Reasoning - Odd One Out

items.explanation: A seed grows into a plant, and an acorn grows into an oak, so both pairs show a thing and what it becomes. An egg is not what a nest becomes, a shell is part of an egg, and wool is part of a sheep rather than what a sheep becomes.
items.question: Seed : Plant bears the relation of a thing to what it becomes. Which of the following pairs bears the same relation?

items.explanation: The lakes that are deep are water bodies, since lakes are water bodies, so some water bodies are deep. Conclusion I does not follow: the water bodies that are lakes need not be rivers.
items.question: Statements: All rivers are water bodies. Some water bodies are lakes. Some lakes are deep. Conclusions: I. Some rivers are deep. II. Some water bodies are deep.

items.explanation: Both moves need patients to act on the information: they must be able and willing to choose a hospital based on waiting time, which is what makes publishing the times useful and online booking worth offering. That patients read information online supports publishing alone, since reading is not choosing. That shorter waits mean better treatment and that waiting times differ do not by themselves make patients choose on waiting time.
options: Patients read information online before choosing
Patients are able and willing to choose a hospital based on waiting time
items.question: A hospital will publish waiting times online, saying patients will choose shorter queues, and will also let patients book appointments online. Which of the following must be assumed for both decisions to make sense?
items.topic: Analytical and Logical Reasoning - Statement and Assumption

items.explanation: One cause explains all three figures if its effects point in different directions: pedestrianisation draws more people, which raises footfall and takings, and the traffic it displaces moves to the surrounding streets, which raises traffic there. The other options reverse the direction or deny any connection.
options: Pedestrianisation brought more people to the area, raising footfall and takings, while the displaced traffic moved to the surrounding streets.
Higher shop takings caused the pedestrianisation.
The three rises are unrelated coincidences.
Rising traffic on the surrounding streets caused footfall to rise.
items.question: After the city pedestrianised the market street, footfall rose, shop takings rose, and traffic on the surrounding streets rose too. Which is the most likely explanation?
items.topic: Analytical and Logical Reasoning - Cause and Effect

items.explanation: The north and south legs partly cancel: 8 km north and 16 km south leave a net 8 km south. With 15 km east, the displacement is the hypotenuse of 8 and 15, which is 17 km, south-east. Adding all three legs gives 39 km, the trap for solvers who treat a route as a straight line, and north-east ignores that the south leg outweighs the north leg.
items.question: A person walks 8 km north, then 15 km east, then 16 km south. How far is the person from the starting point, and in which direction?
items.topic: Analytical and Logical Reasoning - Direction Sense

items.explanation: The unknown distance cancels out. She walks north for the unknown distance, then west for 4 km, then south for the same unknown distance, which returns her to her starting latitude, then east for 4 km, which returns her to her starting longitude. She is back at the starting point, whatever the unknown distance was. Her turns run north, west, south, east, so she ends facing East. Counting only the two 4 km legs, or stopping after the southward leg, gives the wrong position or the wrong facing.
options: 4 km west of the starting point / East
Back at the starting point / East
Back at the starting point / West
4 km east of the starting point / West
items.question: A person walks north for an unknown distance, turns left and walks 4 km, turns left and walks the same unknown distance, then turns left and walks 4 km. Where is she relative to her starting point, and which direction is she facing? Give the position and the direction in order.
items.topic: Analytical and Logical Reasoning - Direction Sense

items.explanation: After the swap C sits in D's old position, 14th from the left. Moving 3 places to the right takes C to position 17 from the left. 14 is C's rank before the extra move, and 23 comes from counting the move from C's original position instead of the swapped one.
items.question: In a row of 36 people, C is 9th from the right. C and D swap places. D was 14th from the left. C then moves 3 places to the right. What is C's rank from the left now?

items.explanation: The clocks drift apart by 10 minutes a day, 6 gained by A and 4 lost by B, so a full hour of difference takes 60 divided by 10, or 6 days, which is Saturday at noon. By then A has gained 6 times 6, or 36 minutes, so it shows 12:36 PM, and B has lost 6 times 4, or 24 minutes, so it shows 11:36 AM. Friday is only 5 days on, when the drift is 50 minutes, and 12:30 PM with 11:30 AM is the reading for a 30-minute gain and loss, not the 36 and 24 the six days give.
options: Saturday noon / A 1:00 PM, B 11:00 AM
Saturday noon / A 12:36 PM, B 11:36 AM
Friday noon / A 12:36 PM, B 11:36 AM
Saturday noon / A 12:30 PM, B 11:30 AM
items.question: Clock A gains 6 minutes a day and clock B loses 4 minutes a day. Both are set right at noon on Sunday. On which day, and at what true time, is clock A first exactly one hour ahead of clock B, and what does each clock then show? Give the day and true time, then the two readings, A first, in order.

items.explanation: The 100th day is 99 days after 1 January, and 99 divided by 7 leaves remainder 1, so it is a Tuesday. The 250th day is 249 days after 1 January, and 249 divided by 7 leaves remainder 4, so it is a Friday. 2024 is a leap year, but the remainder calculation already accounts for the actual day count.
items.question: 1 January 2024 was a Monday. What day of the week was the 100th day of 2024, and what day of the week was the 250th day of 2024? Give the two days in order.

items.explanation: Place the people from the clues: G - E - D - A - F - B - C from left to right. The middle seat is the fourth, which is A. No clue states the middle seat directly: it follows only from combining the left-end clue with the chain of neighbours.
items.passage: Seven people, A, B, C, D, E, F and G, sit in a row facing north. G sits at the left end. E sits immediately to the right of G. D sits immediately to the left of A. A sits second to the right of E. F sits immediately to the right of A. B sits immediately to the left of C. C sits second to the right of F.
items.question: Who sits in the middle of the row?
items.topic: Analytical and Logical Reasoning - Seating Arrangement

items.explanation: The full row is G, E, D, A, F, B, C from left to right, which is determined only by combining all the clues: no single clue fixes more than one seat. D is in position 3, so two places to the right is position 5, which is F. The other options sit next to D or at the wrong distance, and they are the traps for solvers who count one place instead of two.
items.question: Who sits second to the right of D?
items.topic: Analytical and Logical Reasoning - Seating Arrangement

items.explanation: The two changes multiply to 1.25 x 0.9 = 1.125, so the original price is 1125 / 1.125 = Rs 1,000. After only the 25 percent rise the price would have been 1000 x 1.25 = Rs 1,250.
items.question: A price rises by 25 percent, then falls by 10 percent, and ends at Rs 1,125. What was the original price, and what would the price have been after only the rise? Give the original price first, then the price after only the rise.
items.stream_verdict: REBUILD: Mechanical percentage chain: one formula applied three times in succession. One concept, no non-obvious step.

items.explanation: Revenue is 300 x 70 + 100 x 40 = Rs 25,000 against a cost of 400 x 50 = Rs 20,000, so profit is Rs 5,000, or 25%. If all 400 units had sold at Rs 70, revenue would be Rs 28,000, profit Rs 8,000, or 40%. 30% in the first place comes from valuing the last 100 units at Rs 70 as well, and 20% comes from ignoring the units sold below cost.
items.question: A trader buys 400 units at Rs 50 each. He sells 300 units at Rs 70 each and the remaining 100 units at Rs 40 each. What is his profit percentage, and what would it have been if all 400 units had sold at Rs 70 each? Give the two percentages in order.

items.explanation: The principal is 2,000 x 100 / (10 x 2) = Rs 10,000. At 12% for 3 years the interest is 10,000 x 12 x 3 / 100 = Rs 3,600, while at 10% for 3 years it would be Rs 3,000, so the 12% interest is Rs 600 more. Rs 2,400 is the interest for 2 years at 12%, and Rs 4,000 comes from using 4 years instead of 3.
items.question: The simple interest on a sum for 2 years at 10% per annum is Rs 2,000. What is the simple interest on the same sum for 3 years at 12% per annum, and how much more is it than the simple interest on the same sum for 3 years at 10% per annum? Give the two amounts in order.

items.explanation: Interest is 5 percent per half year. After two half years the amount is 10,000 x 1.05 x 1.05 = Rs 11,025. Withdrawing Rs 1,000 leaves Rs 10,025. One more half year at 5 percent gives 10,025 x 1.05 = Rs 10,526.25.
items.question: Rs 10,000 is invested at 10 percent per annum compounded half-yearly. After one year, Rs 1,000 is withdrawn. What is the amount at the end of 1.5 years?

items.explanation: The totals are 10 x 25 = 250, 20 x 55 = 1,100, 10 x 85 = 850 and 10 x 65 = 650, a combined total of 2,850 years across 50 members. The average is 2,850/50 = 57 years.
items.question: Three groups have 10, 20 and 10 members with average ages 25, 55 and 85 years. A fourth group of 10 members with an average age of 65 years joins them. What is the average age of all the members now?

items.explanation: The shifted values sum to 700 minus 150, or 550, and the ratios 1 : 4 and 2 : 3 combine to 1 : 4 : 6, or 11 parts, so each part is 50. Let y - 35 = 200. Then x - 70 = 50 and z - 45 = 300, so x = 120, y = 235 and z = 345, and x + y = 355. The ratios apply to the shifted values, not the originals: applying them to the originals gives 318.18. Solving for x alone gives 120, which answers the wrong question.
items.question: Three numbers x, y and z sum to 700. If x is reduced by 70, y by 35 and z by 45, then (x - 70) : (y - 35) = 1 : 4 and (y - 35) : (z - 45) = 2 : 3. Find x + y.

items.explanation: The speed is 150 / 12 = 12.5 m/s, which is 12.5 x 18 / 5 = 45 km/h. To cross a 150 m platform the train must cover its own length plus the platform, 150 + 150 = 300 m, which at 12.5 m/s takes 300 / 12.5 = 24 seconds. 12 seconds is the time for the pole alone, and 36 km/h comes from using 10 m/s instead of 12.5 m/s.
items.question: A train 150 m long crosses a pole in 12 seconds. What is its speed in km/h, and how many seconds will it take to cross a platform 150 m long? Give the speed and the time in order.

items.explanation: Convert each pair to hourly rates: A + B do 900 / (9 x 5) = 20 units an hour, B + C do 15, and A + C do 15. Solving gives A's rate as 10 units an hour, so A alone needs 900 / (10 x 6) = 15 days at 6 hours a day. Treating days as the unit without rescaling the hours gives 9 days, and forgetting the final hours conversion gives 18 days.
items.question: A and B work 5 hours a day and complete a job in 9 days. B and C work 6 hours a day and complete the same job in 10 days. A and C work 5 hours a day and complete the same job in 12 days. How many days will A take to complete the job alone, working 6 hours a day?

items.explanation: The solution starts with 200 x 0.10 = 20 g of salt. After the first addition it has 70 g of salt in 250 g of solution, which is 28%. After the second addition it has 120 g of salt in 300 g of solution, so the final percentage is 120 / 300 = 40%. 28% stops after the first addition, 35% adds the salt without adding it to the total weight, and 25% comes from adding only 50 g of salt in total.
items.question: 200 g of a salt solution contains 10% salt. 50 g of salt is added. Then another 50 g of salt is added. What is the percentage of salt in the final solution?

items.explanation: P(exactly two heads) is 3/8, since the outcomes are HHT, HTH and THH out of 8 equally likely outcomes. P(at least one head) is 1 - P(no heads) = 1 - 1/8 = 7/8. The conditional probability is (3/8) / (7/8) = 3/7. 3/8 is the unconditional probability, the trap for solvers who ignore the given information, and 1/2 counts the outcomes with two or more heads out of the wrong set.
items.question: Three fair coins are tossed. Given that at least one head appears, what is the probability of getting exactly two heads?

items.explanation: Weight each group by its die probability and by its share of girls: the joint probabilities are 1/8, 1/12, 5/18, so the total probability of a girl is 35/72. By Bayes, the probability of group Z given a girl is 5/18 / 35/72 = 4/7. 9/35 and 6/35 are the Bayes figures for the other two groups, and 5/12 is the unweighted share of girls in group Z, the trap for solvers who skip the die weights.
items.question: A group is chosen by rolling a fair die: the roll gives group X with probability 1/6, group Y with probability 1/6 and group Z with probability 2/3. group X has 3 girls and 1 boy; group Y has 2 girls and 2 boys; group Z has 5 girls and 7 boys. A child is then picked at random from the chosen group and turns out to be a girl. What is the probability that she was picked from group Z?

items.explanation: Without the order rule there are 144 arrangements with the vowels in the odd positions: choose 2 of the 3 odd positions for A and E, in 3 x 2 = 6 ways, and arrange the 4 consonants in the remaining 4 places, in 4! = 24 ways. Requiring C before L keeps exactly half of them, since C and L are equally likely to come first, so the count is 144 / 2 = 72. 144 is the trap for solvers who apply the vowel rule but forget the order rule, and 104 comes from applying a non-adjacency rule that this item does not ask for.
items.question: In how many ways can the letters of CANDLE be arranged so that the vowels occupy only the odd positions and the letter C appears before the letter L?

items.explanation: Statement I is true: same-colour pairs number C(4,2) + C(3,2) + C(2,2) = 6 + 3 + 1 = 10 out of C(9,2) = 36 pairs, and 10/36 = 5/18. Statement II is false: after one red ball is drawn, 3 red balls remain out of 8, so the probability is 3/8, not 1/3, and 1/3 is what you get by forgetting to remove the drawn ball. Statement III is true: given the first ball is not blue, the first ball is one of the 6 red or green balls, and 3 blue balls remain out of the 8 left, so the probability is 3/8; the conditioning removes the blue-first cases symmetrically. Only I and III are true.
items.question: A bag contains 4 red, 3 blue and 2 green balls. Two balls are drawn one after another without replacement. Consider the following statements. I. The probability that both balls are the same colour is 5/18. II. Given that the first ball is red, the probability that the second ball is red is 1/3. III. Given that the first ball is not blue, the probability that the second ball is blue is 3/8. Select the option that lists all and only the true statements.
items.stream_verdict: OLD: Three probability statements on three draws, where the difficulty was counting ordered triples under a conditioning event. NEW: Three probability statements on two draws, each testing a different conditional error: same-colour counting, forgetting the removed ball, and conditioning on a negated event. COLD-SOLVE: Enumeration verified: I = 10/36 = 5/18; II = 3/8 (claimed 1/3 false); III = 3/8 by ordered-pair enumeration. Unique key C.

items.explanation: Combining the logarithms gives log2 of x(x - 6) = 3, so x squared - 6x = 8, which is x squared - 6x - 8 = 0. Solving gives x = 3 + root 17 or x = 3 - root 17. The second root is negative, and the logarithm also needs x greater than 6, so only 3 + root 17, about 7.12, is valid.
items.question: Solve for x: log2(x) + log2(x - 6) = 3.

items.explanation: The 45-degree angle gives AB = CD + BC = 6 + 8 = 14 cm, because the horizontal offset equals the height. Area is then (14 + 6) / 2 x 8 = 80 sq cm. 112 sq cm treats the trapezium as a rectangle of sides AB and BC, and 20 cm for AB adds both bases instead of adding the height to the shorter base.
items.question: In a trapezium, AB is parallel to CD, angle ABC is 90 degrees and angle BAD is 45 degrees. CD is 6 cm and BC is 8 cm. Find the area of the trapezium and the length AB. Give the area and the length in order.

items.explanation: The lights meet every LCM(30, 40, 60) = 120 seconds. The first joint change after 10:00:00 AM is at 10:02:00 AM, the second at 10:04:00 AM, and the third at 10:06:00 AM. 10:02:00 AM is the trap for solvers who stop at the first joint change, and 10:04:00 AM stops at the second.
items.question: Three traffic lights change at intervals of 30, 40 and 60 seconds. If all three change together at 10:00:00 AM, at what time will they change together for the third time after that?

items.explanation: Statement I alone says x cubed minus x is greater than 0, which factors as x(x - 1)(x + 1) greater than 0, so x lies in (-1, 0) or in (1, infinity). In (-1, 0), x squared is less than 1, and in (1, infinity) it is greater than 1, so statement I does not settle the question. Statement II alone only says x is greater than 0, and x squared exceeds 1 exactly when x exceeds 1, so it does not settle it either. Together they force x into (1, infinity), where x squared is greater than 1, so both statements together are sufficient.
options: Neither statement alone nor together is sufficient
items.question: Is x squared greater than 1? Statement I: x cubed is greater than x. Statement II: x is greater than 0.

items.explanation: Above the index is 75% of the population, and males are 2 of every 3 of that slice, so males above the index are 50% of the total. Total is therefore 1.5 / 0.5 = 3 lakh. The below-index ratio is a decoy: using it gives 10 lakh, and treating 25% as the above-index share gives a still different figure.
items.question: The male population above the educational index in Uttar Pradesh is 1.5 lakh. Find the total population of Uttar Pradesh, approximately.

items.explanation: Males below the index are 10% of the population times 3 of 5, or 6% of the whole population, and males above it are 90% times 4 of 5, or 72% of the whole population. Total males are therefore 78% of the population, and the below-index share of males is 6 divided by 78, or 7.69%. 10% is the share of the whole population below the index, not of males, 6% is the below-index males as a share of the whole population rather than of males, and 92.31% is the share of males above the index, which answers the opposite question.
items.question: What is the male population below the educational index in Madhya Pradesh as a percentage of the total male population of Madhya Pradesh?

diagram.caption: Epsilon Ltd: revenue and cost (Rs crore)

items.explanation: Profit margin is (revenue - cost) / revenue. The margins are 2019: 18.18%; 2020: 15.38%; 2021: 17.65%; 2022: 22.73%. The highest is 2022 at 22.73%. 2019 has the second-highest margin, and the year with the largest revenue is not the year with the highest margin, since margin depends on the gap between revenue and cost, not on revenue alone.
items.question: Epsilon Ltd's revenue and cost are shown in the chart. In which year was the profit margin (profit as a percentage of revenue) the highest, and what was that margin? Give the year and the margin in order.

items.explanation: The manager has asked directly whether you know of any leak, so you must answer truthfully now: staying silent, warning the colleague privately, or waiting for a repeat leak all leave the leak undisclosed and the client exposed, and giving the colleague a day to self-report would mean withholding the truth from a direct question. Only telling the manager the truth now discharges both the duty to protect the client and the duty to tell the truth.
options: Say nothing to the manager and warn the colleague privately to be more careful.
Confront the colleague and insist they stop, but tell the manager nothing.
Disclose it to the manager only if the leak happens again.
Tell the manager the truth now about the leak.
items.question: You discover that a colleague has been sharing a client's confidential pricing with a rival firm. The colleague is a friend, admits it when you ask, and begs you to keep it quiet, promising to stop. Your manager then asks you directly whether you know of any leak of client information. What should you do?
items.stream_verdict: OLD: Single-rule ethics: refuse a facilitation fee, correct the official, escalate, address the report. NEW: Conflicting-duties ethics: loyalty to a friend versus truth to a manager and protection of a client, resolved by a self-report window plus disclosure. COLD-SOLVE: Cold solve: only option B discharges both duties; A and C conceal, D makes disclosure conditional on a repeat.

items.explanation: Filing from a work device the manager monitors would expose you before the complaint is even read, so the channel's postal route exists for exactly this situation. Only the first option protects you and the evidence: the records are gathered, the complaint goes by post, and a copy of your filing is kept outside the office. Confronting the manager and accepting an apology leaves the false claims uncorrected and exposes you to retaliation, telling the whole team spreads an allegation before any process has run, and ignoring it because the allowance is small lets the size of the sum decide a matter of falsified records.
options: Gather the records, file the matter with the whistleblower channel by post, and keep a copy of your filing outside the office
Ignore it, since the allowance is small
Confront your manager and accept an apology
Tell the whole team what you found
items.question: You find that your manager has been falsifying attendance records to claim an allowance. You have the records to prove it. The manager is also the person who signs your appraisal, and the allowance is small. The whistleblower channel accepts complaints by post, and the manager monitors the work devices. What should you do?

items.explanation: Communication is a real criterion for this role, so ignoring the mark removes it instead of applying it fairly, and leaving the earlier mark in place judges the candidate twice, once fairly and once on accent. The panel's claim is about clarity, and clarity can be tested: a customer-call simulation shows whether customers can actually follow the candidate. Only the second option assesses the content, tests clarity on the simulation, and asks the panel to rescore on that evidence alone.
options: Mark the candidate down for communication, since the panel already did
Assess the content of the answers, test clarity with a real customer-call simulation, and ask the panel to rescore the communication mark on the simulation alone
Assess the content but leave the earlier communication mark as it is
items.question: A candidate speaks with a strong regional accent. Their answers are clear and well structured. The panel has already marked the candidate down for communication. The role needs clear spoken communication with customers, and the panel argues the accent itself affects clarity. How should you assess them?

items.explanation: Stopping the claims for the future does not cover the deals already signed, which contain the false claims in writing, so the clients who signed them are still exposed. Letting sales continue waits for the complaints to arrive, and dismissing the salesperson without checking the deals skips the process and leaves the signed deals unchecked. Only the third option stops the claims, retrains the salesperson, audits the signed deals, discloses the false claims to the affected clients, and sets consequences.
options: Let the sales continue, since clients have not complained
Stop the claims but say nothing to the clients who already signed
Stop the claims, retrain the salesperson, audit the signed deals, disclose the false claims to the affected clients, and set consequences
Dismiss the salesperson at once without checking the deals
items.question: Your best salesperson wins deals by making claims about the product that are not true. Clients have not complained yet. The deals already signed contain the false claims in writing, so the clients can claim misrepresentation. What should you do?

items.explanation: Meeting the collector's 30% target would breach the cooling system's safety minimum, so the target cannot be met as stated, however reasonable it looks. Refusing to cut at all lets output decide a matter of shared water in a drought, and cutting without a published plan leaves the community unable to check the cut. Only the fourth option cuts as far as safety allows, explains the shortfall to the collector with the safety evidence, publishes a reduction plan, and offsets the rest by recycling.
options: Refuse to cut, since production would fall
Cut water use, meet the collector's target, publish a reduction plan, and share progress with the community
Cut water use but publish no plan
Cut use to the safety minimum, explain the shortfall to the collector with the safety evidence, publish a reduction plan, and offset the rest by recycling water
items.question: Your plant uses a lot of water in a district facing drought. Cutting use will slow production. The district collector has asked for a 30% cut, and production would fall by a fifth. The plant's cooling system needs a minimum flow, and a 30% cut would breach that safety minimum. What should you do?

items.explanation: The fees being lawful under clause 14 does not answer the regulator's warning, which is about prominence, and it does not help the customers who found the fees only on their first statement. Refunding quietly without disclosing the fees upfront keeps the next customers in the dark, and disclosing the fees while refusing refunds leaves the affected customers out of pocket. Only the first option discloses all fees upfront, reissues clear statements, refunds the fees charged without clear disclosure, and replies to the warning.
options: Disclose all fees upfront, reissue clear statements, refund fees charged without clear disclosure, and reply to the regulator's warning
Keep the fees in the fine print, since most customers do not notice
Disclose the fees but refuse refunds
Refund quietly without disclosing the fees upfront
items.question: Your loan product has fees that appear only in the fine print. Most customers do not notice them until the first statement. The regulator has just warned firms about hidden fees. The fees were charged under contracts that disclose them in clause 14, so the charges are lawful, but the regulator's warning is about prominence, not legality. What should you do?

items.explanation: The evidence is partial, so it must be verified independently rather than acted on as proven or ignored, and the contract allows suspension only on verified evidence, so existing orders cannot be suspended on undated photographs. The regulator's 7-day rule is non-negotiable, so the suspicion must be reported on time and labelled unverified. Only the fourth option fits all three facts at once: commission an independent verification within the week, report the suspicion as unverified within 7 days, and pause new orders while keeping contracted orders running until the check concludes. Suspending everything breaches the contract and leaves 200 workers unpaid on evidence that has not been verified, and a public accusation asserts guilt before the facts are tested. Doing nothing misses the reporting deadline, and asking the supplier to investigate itself is not verification.
options: Suspend all orders at once and announce publicly that the supplier has broken the law
Do nothing until the photographs are proved genuine
Ask the supplier to investigate itself and accept whatever it reports

Commission an independent verification of the photographs and the site within the week, report the suspicion to the regulator as unverified within 7 days, and pause new orders while keeping contracted orders running until the check concludes
items.question: Your supplier is suspected of clearing protected forest. A local group has sent you photographs that appear to show the clearing, but the photographs are undated and do not identify the location, and the supplier denies any clearing. Your contract allows you to suspend a supplier only on verified evidence of a breach, and suspending all orders now would breach the contract and leave 200 workers unpaid. The regulator requires any suspected breach to be reported within 7 days. What should you do?

items.explanation: The offer expires today but the quotes take three days, so the deadline is a pressure tactic, not a reason to accept half the cost without evidence. Demanding the full cost at once without agreeing it breaks the relationship over a sum that can be settled, and going to court spends more on the dispute than the repair costs. Only the second option accepts the principle of payment, gets two quotes to settle the amount, and agrees it together, so the neighbour pays a fair cost and the relationship survives.
options: Accept half the cost without any quotes
Accept the principle of payment, get two repair quotes over three days, agree the amount together, and settle on the quotes rather than the expiring offer
Demand the full cost at once without agreeing it
Refuse any payment and go to court
items.question: A neighbour's dog damaged your garden. The neighbour offers a small sum that covers half the repair cost. The neighbour denies the dog did it, and the repair costs twice the sum offered. The neighbour's offer expires today, and repair quotes take three days. What should you do?
items.topic: Ethics - Personal Morality and Civic Responsibility

items.explanation: Reassuring them that they will pass hides the truth two weeks before the exam, and telling them they will fail without a plan leaves them knowing the outcome without a way to change it. The resit in six months is a fallback, not a reason to give up on the two weeks, since sitting the exam unprepared wastes the attempt. Only the third option tells them honestly where they stand, agrees a plan with daily targets, and keeps the resit as the fallback if the plan slips.
options: Reassure them that they will pass
Tell them honestly but offer no plan
Tell them honestly where they stand, agree a plan to improve, set daily targets for the two weeks, and keep the resit as a fallback if the plan slips
Tell them they will fail and leave it there
items.question: A student asks whether they will pass. You believe they will probably fail unless they change how they study. The exam is in two weeks, and the student has not started revising. The student has a resit option in six months. What should you say?
items.topic: Ethics - Personal Morality and Civic Responsibility

items.explanation: The gift has already been sent to your home, so refusing it in words is not enough: it must be returned, or it stays with you. Accepting it because the loan is deserved creates an obligation and a precedent, however sound the loan is. Reporting the applicant to the police treats a misjudged gesture as a crime, and delaying the loan to teach a lesson punishes an applicant whose loan meets every criterion. Only the first option returns the gift, processes the loan on its merits, records the offer, and tells the applicant the practice is not accepted.
options: Return the gift, refuse it, process the loan on its merits, record the offer, and tell the applicant the practice is not accepted
Accept the gift, since the loan is deserved anyway
Report the applicant to the police
Refuse the gift but delay the loan to teach the applicant a lesson
items.question: You are a loan officer. An applicant offers you a gift to speed up approval of a loan that already meets every criterion. The applicant says every officer accepts such gifts. The applicant has already sent the gift to your home address. What should you do?
items.topic: Ethics - Personal Morality and Civic Responsibility
